paras: The Needmore whitecap raid was a night attack by a masked band of fifteen to thirty "whitecaps" on the home of John Millikin, a Black preacher, at Needmore, a Black settlement near Lewisburg in Marshall County, Tennessee, after midnight on August 3–4, 1903. Millikin was shot dead as he fled, and his son-in-law John Hunter was shot in the back after the band forced him to join a search; Hunter was first reported mortally wounded and later as killed. No cause was known, the governor offered a $500 reward, and year-end chronologies in Black and white papers listed the case among the lynchings of 1903.

Needmore, east of Lewisburg in Marshall County, was described as a settlement "inhabited almost exclusively by negroes." Millikin was a preacher; Hunter, who slept in his house, was a cook recently back from Nashville, where he had worked at Kissam Hall, Vanderbilt University. A Nashville dispatch added that Millikin's reputation "in some respects was not of the best" and that he had said that day he was not going to be killed.

Between midnight and one o'clock disguised men, mostly mounted and some in buggies, reached Millikin's house. Once the door was open they demanded a light; Millikin told his wife not to strike a match, but she did, and he slipped out the back door. Ordered to halt, he kept running until a volley brought him down; nine bullet holes were found in his body.

The band then took Hunter in charge and asked him where Dave Turner, another Black man, could be found. When he said he did not know, they forced him along on a fruitless search. In what the New York Sun called his dying statement, Hunter said he thought they were going to kill him anyway, so he broke away and was shot in the back. Millikin's wife was struck over the head with a gun, and witnesses said the raiders were young men or boys, with one exception.

Coroner Bowden's jury viewed the remains and found the men shot by "a masked mob unknown to the jury." Hunter was reported "in a dying condition" on August 5; no notice of his death appears, though later reports counted him among the dead.

Otis Fowler, charged with taking part in the raid, was tried on August 6 before Squires Hill and Coffman, and in a ten-minute hearing he proved that he had been in Nashville at the time. Governor Frazier offered a $500 reward, which the Columbia Herald called "larger than customary" but deserved "by reason of the nature of the crime." The Nashville Banner reported the raid "strongly denounced" by law-abiding people of the county; no further arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The first wire report, printed on August 4 in Walla Walla and Spokane, said two Black men had been "riddled with bullets and buckshot"; the Spokane Press headed it "Whitecaps Shoot Unoffending Negroes." On August 5 a fuller wire story naming the victims ran in New York, Indianapolis, Alexandria and Rock Island, and a Nashville Banner special with the inquest verdict appeared in Birmingham and Louisville. Headlines included "Whitecappers Kill Preacher" and "Murderous Whitecappers"; the Birmingham Age-Herald's reversed the victims. Weekly digests cut the story to a line, as in the Washington Evening Star's "A mob at Needmore, Tenn., killed a negro preacher," and the Chicago Eagle called it "the lynching."

Black papers carried the wire text with little added: the Kansas City American Citizen headed it "Mob Shot a Negro Preacher No Reason Assigned," and the Savannah Tribune ran it as "Whitecappers in Tennessee." The St. Paul Appeal, in editorial notes following President Roosevelt's letter on lawlessness, said a preacher had been lynched at Lewisburg "on general principles." At the year's end the Chicago Broad Ax, printing the same chronology that ran in white papers, listed Millikin and Hunter under "Lynchings" as "killed by whitecappers."

Reports disagree on Hunter's fate: the earliest wire spoke of two men killed, the August 5–8 accounts called him mortally wounded, and the Columbia Herald of August 14 and the year-end chronologies counted both as killed. The preacher's name also appears as Milliken, Milligan and "Green Milligan."

reader.title: Needmore whitecap raid
bases: A masked whitecap band of fifteen to thirty raided a Black settlement at night, shot John Millikin dead and shot John Hunter in the back after forcing him on a search (A5, A12), and contemporaries listed it among the year's lynchings (A36, A45).

Millikin was killed by a band of fifteen to thirty disguised whitecaps acting without any authority (A5, A12); no cause was stated, but the band acted as night 'whitecaps' hunting another Black man in a Black settlement, the regulator tradition, and Black and white papers classed it as a lynching (A12, A43, A45).

Independent dispatches from Lewisburg and Nashville (A2, A8, A10, A12) and a nearby Tennessee weekly (A30, A42) agree on the raid and Millikin's killing; only Hunter's death is reported inconsistently.

accounts.label: Early Lewisburg wire (Aug. 4)
accounts.gist: White Caps invaded Needmore after midnight; two Black men called from their houses were riddled with bullets and buckshot as they fled; neither had committed any crime; the coroner found death from an unknown mob.

accounts.label: Standard wire (Aug. 5)
accounts.gist: Fifteen to thirty whitecappers came to preacher John Millikin's home; he was killed fleeing; son-in-law John Hunter was forced on a search and fatally shot in the back; the wife was struck; no cause assigned.

accounts.label: Nashville dispatches and Banner special
accounts.gist: Add the demand for a light, nine bullet holes, Hunter's dying statement, the search for Dave Turner, the inquest verdict, local denunciation, and that the band were young men or boys.

accounts.label: Columbia Herald (Tenn.)
accounts.gist: Otis Fowler, charged with taking part, proved an alibi on Aug. 6; on Aug. 14 the paper reported the governor's $500 reward and called both men shot to death.

accounts.label: Black editorial comment
accounts.gist: The St. Paul Appeal said a preacher had been lynched 'on general principles'; the Broad Ax chronology listed both men as killed by whitecappers.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Whitecaps Shoot Unoffending Negroes' and 'Murderous Whitecappers'; text stresses neither man 'committed any crime' and both bore good reputations.
Most papers ran the standard wire or a one-line digest ('A mob at Needmore, Tenn., killed a negro preacher').
The Columbia Herald said the larger-than-customary reward would 'meet with general approbation by reason of the nature of the crime'.
American Citizen ('Mob Shot a Negro Preacher No Reason Assigned') and Savannah Tribune ('Whitecappers in Tennessee') reprinted the wire without comment.
St. Paul Appeal set the case among editorial notes on lawlessness, calling it a lynching 'on general principles'.

versions.value: Millikin killed, Hunter fatally or mortally wounded, 'in a dying condition'

conflicts.note: The Aug. 14 Columbia Herald, a nearby Tennessee paper writing ten days later, is the latest local word and says both died, but it reports no death or funeral; the early two-dead wire predates the fuller accounts that had Hunter alive.
Spelling variants of the same preacher; the Age-Herald headline also reverses the victims ('Hunter is dead and Millikin fatally wounded') against its own text (A10).
Minor; likely a transcription difference in the Banner special.
